title: Apache Cassandra Internals
summary: Apache Cassandra is a distributed, wide-column NoSQL database designed for high-availability and linear horizontal scalability. Its masterless architecture (consistent hashing ring, gossip protocol, tunable consistency), LSM-tree storage engine (memtable + SSTable), and partition-key-centric data model make it the right choice for high-write-throughput, geographically distributed workloads where availability trumps strict consistency.

sections.title: Architecture: Masterless Ring and Consistent Hashing
paragraphs: Cassandra has no master node—every node in the cluster is functionally identical (peer-to-peer). This masterless design is the source of Cassandra's high availability: there's no single point of failure, no election needed during failure, and no primary-replica failover latency. Data is distributed across nodes using consistent hashing: each row's partition key is hashed to a position on a virtual ring; each node is responsible for a range of that ring. With virtual nodes (vnodes), each physical node hosts multiple small token ranges, enabling smooth data distribution without manual token assignment.

The gossip protocol maintains cluster membership: each node gossips with 1-3 random peers every second, exchanging cluster state (which nodes are up/down, their token assignments, schema versions). Within seconds, a node failure is detected and propagated cluster-wide without central coordination. The gossip protocol also drives the anti-entropy repair process: nodes compare their data with peers and exchange missing or mismatched rows, maintaining eventual consistency over time.

Replication is configured per keyspace with a replication factor (RF). With RF=3, each row is stored on 3 consecutive nodes in the ring. The replica placement strategy (NetworkTopologyStrategy) ensures replicas are placed on different racks and data centers for failure domain isolation. When a client writes, it contacts any node (the coordinator). The coordinator routes the write to all responsible replicas (determined by the partition key's position on the ring).

Tunable consistency: each read and write operation specifies its consistency level. CL.ONE: single replica acknowledgment (fastest, least consistent). CL.QUORUM: majority of replicas (RF/2+1) must acknowledge. CL.ALL: all replicas must acknowledge (slowest, most consistent). For strong consistency, use CL.QUORUM for both reads and writes—this ensures at least one node participated in both the latest write and the read, guaranteeing read-after-write. CL.LOCAL_QUORUM limits acknowledgment to the local datacenter, providing low-latency strong consistency within a region.
bullets: Masterless ring: every node equal; no primary/replica failover; no SPOF
Consistent hashing: partition key → token position → responsible nodes
Vnodes: each physical node holds N virtual token ranges; smooth load distribution
Tunable consistency: CL.ONE (AP), CL.QUORUM (CP), CL.LOCAL_QUORUM (regional CP)

sections.title: LSM-Tree Storage: Memtable, SSTable, and Compaction
paragraphs: Cassandra's storage engine is an LSM (Log-Structured Merge-tree). Writes go first to an in-memory data structure (memtable) and a commit log (write-ahead log for durability). When the memtable reaches a size threshold, it is flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable (Sorted String Table). SSTables are never modified—updates and deletes create new versions. This design makes writes extremely fast (memory + sequential disk write) but requires periodic compaction to merge SSTables and remove obsolete versions.

An SSTable consists of several files: data file (actual column values, compressed), index file (partition key → data file offset), summary file (sample of index for in-memory range lookup), statistics file (partition count, min/max column values), and bloom filter file (probabilistic index to skip SSTables that definitely don't contain the requested partition key). On a read, Cassandra checks the bloom filter of each SSTable, then consults the summary and index to find the partition's location in the data file.

Tombstones are Cassandra's delete mechanism. Because SSTables are immutable, DELETE doesn't remove data—it writes a tombstone marker. The tombstone is replicated to all replicas. During compaction, tombstones older than gc_grace_seconds (default: 10 days) are physically removed. This gc_grace_seconds is the window for deleted data to propagate to all replicas before the tombstone can be safely removed—if a replica was down for longer than gc_grace_seconds and misses a delete, the deleted data could resurrect when the replica rejoins (zombie data).

Compaction strategies control how SSTables are merged. SizeTieredCompaction (default): merges similar-sized SSTables; good for write-heavy workloads, creates large SSTables that are slow to read. LeveledCompaction: maintains SSTables in levels where each level is 10x larger than the previous; better read performance (guaranteed to check at most L levels), more I/O-intensive writes. TimeWindowCompaction (TWCS): groups SSTables by time window; ideal for time-series data where old data is never updated. TWCS minimizes compaction I/O by never compacting windows that contain only old, immutable data.
bullets: Writes: memtable (in-memory) + commit log (WAL); flush to SSTable when memtable full
SSTable: immutable; bloom filter + index + data; multiple SSTables merged during compaction
Tombstone: delete marker; physically removed after gc_grace_seconds during compaction
TWCS: time-series compaction; ideal for append-only time-series data

sections.title: Data Modeling: Partition Key, Clustering Columns, and Denormalization
paragraphs: Cassandra's data model is fundamentally query-driven: define your queries first, then design tables to serve those queries exactly. This is the opposite of relational modeling (normalize first, query however you need). Each Cassandra table is a distributed sorted map: the partition key determines which nodes hold the data (hash-based), and the clustering columns determine the sort order within a partition. Queries must specify the partition key (equality or IN clause); range queries are allowed only on clustering columns within a known partition.

Partition design is the most critical modeling decision. A partition holds all rows with the same partition key—they're stored together, read together, and must fit on a single node. Hot partitions (one partition receiving disproportionate reads/writes) become throughput bottlenecks and can cause node instability. Max recommended partition size is 100MB (soft limit); larger partitions cause GC pressure and slow compaction. For user event tables, partition by user_id groups all events per user together—ideal for per-user queries but creates uneven distribution for 'celebrity' users with millions of events. Add a time bucket (toStartOfMonth(event_time)) to bound partition size.

Denormalization is required because Cassandra doesn't support joins or multi-partition queries efficiently. Store the same data in multiple tables, each optimized for a different query pattern. An order system: orders_by_user (partition: user_id, cluster: created_at DESC for recent orders), orders_by_status (partition: status, cluster: created_at for work queue pattern), orders_by_id (partition: order_id for direct lookup). These three tables serve three different access patterns from the same underlying data.

Light transactions (LWT) provide linearizable compare-and-set within a single partition: INSERT INTO locks (key) VALUES ('value') IF NOT EXISTS implements a distributed lock. LWT uses Paxos under the hood—4 round-trips for a successful operation. This is 10-20x slower than a regular write (~5ms vs. ~0.5ms). Use LWT sparingly for idempotency keys and distributed locks where correctness is critical; avoid it in the hot path. For most uniqueness requirements, use Cassandra's partition key structure to enforce uniqueness naturally.
bullets: Query-first design: design table schema around specific queries, not normalized data model
Partition key: determines node placement; must be specified in every query
Clustering columns: sort order within partition; range queries allowed within partition
Denormalization: duplicate data in multiple tables; each optimized for one query pattern

sections.title: Consistency, Hinted Handoff, and Read Repair
paragraphs: Hinted handoff is Cassandra's mechanism for handling temporary node failures without sacrificing write availability. When a replica node is temporarily unavailable, the coordinator stores the write as a 'hint' locally. When the unavailable node returns, the coordinator replays all stored hints. This allows writes to succeed at CL.ONE even when target replicas are temporarily offline—at the cost of eventual consistency for reads until hints are replayed. Hinted handoff has a TTL (default 3 hours); hints older than the TTL are discarded, requiring repair to reconcile the replica.

Read repair reconciles inconsistencies detected during reads. When a read with CL.QUORUM returns different values from different replicas, Cassandra determines the most recent value (using timestamps) and asynchronously writes the correct value back to the stale replica. Read repair is a background correction mechanism—it doesn't slow down the read path (unless using read_repair=blocking which synchronously waits for repair). Over time, read repair converges all replicas to consistent state, but explicit nodetool repair is required for comprehensive reconciliation.

Repair is the most important operational responsibility in Cassandra. Without regular repair, replicas drift: a node that was down and missed hinted handoff (or hints expired) has stale/missing data. nodetool repair initiates an anti-entropy repair using Merkle tree comparison—each node computes a Merkle hash of its data, compares with peer replicas, and exchanges only the differing rows. Full repair must run more frequently than gc_grace_seconds to prevent zombie data resurrection. Many teams use a reaper tool (Cassandra Reaper) to schedule and monitor repair jobs across the cluster.
bullets: Hinted handoff: coordinator stores write for unavailable replica; replays on return
Read repair: reconcile stale replicas detected during quorum reads; asynchronous
nodetool repair: Merkle tree anti-entropy repair; must run more frequently than gc_grace_seconds
Cassandra Reaper: automated repair scheduling and monitoring for production clusters

core.title: Architecture and Consistency
paragraphs: Masterless ring with consistent hashing. Gossip for cluster membership. RF=3 with NetworkTopologyStrategy for DC isolation.
Tunable consistency: CL.ONE (high availability), CL.QUORUM (strong), CL.LOCAL_QUORUM (regional strong).
Vnodes: each node holds N token ranges; smooth load distribution without manual token assignment.
bullets: No SPOF: masterless; any node can serve any request
QUORUM + QUORUM: guarantees read-after-write consistency
LOCAL_QUORUM: strong consistency within datacenter; low-latency

core.title: LSM Storage and Data Modeling
paragraphs: Writes: memtable + commit log → SSTable flush. SSTables immutable; compaction merges them and removes tombstones.
Design tables around queries: partition key for placement, clustering columns for sort order. No joins, no cross-partition queries.
Denormalize: duplicate data in multiple tables, each serving a specific query pattern.
bullets: TWCS: time-series data; compaction by time window; minimal I/O for old data
Tombstones: delete markers; removed after gc_grace_seconds; run repair before gc_grace expires
Partition size: max 100MB; add time bucket to bound growing partitions

deepDive.title: Cassandra Performance Tuning
paragraphs: Read performance bottlenecks: too many SSTables per read (use LeveledCompaction), tombstone accumulation (review delete patterns), large partitions (sub-partition by time), missing or ineffective bloom filters (tune false positive rate). Write performance bottlenecks: compaction falling behind (increase concurrent_compactors), JVM GC pauses (use G1GC with 8-16GB heap, enable incremental compaction), disk I/O saturation (NVMe SSDs mandatory for production).

JVM tuning for Cassandra: use G1GC with -Xms16g -Xmx16g (heap size; don't exceed 32GB to avoid GC pause issues), -XX:+UseStringDeduplication, and -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=500. The off-heap memory (Cassandra uses off-heap for bloom filters, page cache, and compression buffers) often exceeds heap—a node may use 32GB heap + 48GB off-heap = 80GB total. Plan server RAM accordingly: typically 128-256GB RAM per Cassandra node for production workloads.

Cassandra's nodetool utility is the primary operational tool: nodetool status (cluster health), nodetool tpstats (thread pool statistics—critical for detecting backpressure), nodetool cfstats (per-table statistics including read/write latency and SSTable count), nodetool compactionstats (ongoing compaction progress), nodetool repair (trigger manual repair). Monitor tpstats for dropped mutations (indicator of overload) and pending tasks in native transport stage (indicates client backpressure).
bullets: LeveledCompaction: better read performance; each read checks at most L+1 SSTables
G1GC with 16GB heap: stable latency; avoid >32GB heap for Cassandra (long GC pauses)
nodetool tpstats: dropped mutations = overload indicator; monitor pending native transport
SSTable count per read: high count → compaction falling behind → read latency increases

expert.title: Cassandra Multi-Region Active-Active
paragraphs: Cassandra's masterless architecture natively supports multi-region active-active replication. With NetworkTopologyStrategy and RF=3 per datacenter (US-East: 3, EU-West: 3), every write is replicated to 3 nodes in each datacenter. Using CL.LOCAL_QUORUM, writes acknowledge from the local datacenter only, with asynchronous replication to other datacenters. Read latency stays local; write conflicts are resolved by last-write-wins (highest timestamp wins) with no coordination overhead.

Last-write-wins (LWW) conflict resolution requires synchronized clocks. Cassandra uses wall-clock timestamps for conflict resolution—if two datacenters write to the same cell concurrently, the write with the highest timestamp wins. Clock skew can cause recent writes to be lost if the clocks diverge significantly. Use NTP with <1ms skew, or use client-side timestamps controlled by the application to ensure monotonicity. For use cases where LWW is incorrect (counter updates, inventory), use Cassandra Lightweight Transactions (Paxos) or move the conflicting data out of Cassandra.

Change Data Capture (CDC) in Cassandra 3.0+: a cdc_raw directory receives commit log segments when CDC is enabled per table (WITH cdc = true). A separate process (Kafka Cassandra CDC connector, Debezium) reads these commit log segments and publishes row changes to Kafka. This enables Cassandra to participate in event-driven architectures, feeding downstream systems with row-level change events without application-layer dual writes.

concepts: Masterless ring: peer-to-peer; consistent hashing for partition placement; no SPOF
Gossip protocol: peer-to-peer cluster state propagation; detects failures within seconds
Tunable consistency: CL.ONE (AP), CL.QUORUM (CP), CL.LOCAL_QUORUM (regional CP)
Memtable: in-memory write buffer; flushed to SSTable on size threshold
SSTable: immutable sorted disk file; bloom filter + index + data; compaction merges multiple SSTables
Tombstone: delete marker; physically removed after gc_grace_seconds during compaction
Hinted handoff: coordinator stores writes for unavailable replicas; replays on return
Read repair: stale replicas updated asynchronously when discrepancy detected during reads
Partition key: determines node placement via consistent hash; must be in every query
Clustering columns: sort order within a partition; range queries allowed within partition
LWT (Lightweight Transactions): Paxos-based compare-and-set; 4 round-trips; linearizable
TimeWindowCompaction: group SSTables by time; ideal for time-series append workloads
practices: Design tables query-first: define access patterns before schema; create one table per query pattern
Use NetworkTopologyStrategy with RF=3 per datacenter; ensure racks are defined for fault domain isolation
Use TWCS for time-series tables; ensure no cross-window updates to avoid compaction inefficiency
Run nodetool repair more frequently than gc_grace_seconds to prevent zombie data resurrection
Bound partition size with a time bucket in the partition key (toStartOfMonth) for high-volume entities
Monitor tombstone counts with cfstats; excessive tombstones cause 'tombstone_warn_threshold' warnings and read latency
Use CL.LOCAL_QUORUM for multi-region setups to achieve strong consistency within a region at local latency
pitfalls: Using ALLOW FILTERING in queries—full partition scan; indicates missing table design for the access pattern
Using a low-cardinality partition key (status='PENDING')—hot partition that overwhelms 1-2 nodes
Not running repair—replicas drift; deleted data resurrects after gc_grace_seconds expires
Storing large BLOBs (video, images) in Cassandra—causes GC pressure and large partition sizes; use object storage
Overusing LWT for uniqueness checks—4 round-trips; use partition key design to enforce uniqueness naturally
Not monitoring compaction—when compaction falls behind, SSTable count grows; read latency degrades severely
No time-to-live (TTL) on ephemeral data—tombstones accumulate indefinitely if TTL-based deletion is not used

examples.title: Netflix View History
examples.description: Netflix uses Cassandra to store viewing history for 300 million users. The table is partitioned by user_id with clustering columns (profile_id, timestamp DESC) to serve 'get last N watched titles per profile' queries. RF=3 per datacenter (US-East, EU-West, AP-Southeast) with CL.LOCAL_QUORUM ensures strong per-region consistency. TWCS compaction handles the time-series append workload efficiently—older viewing history is never updated, so old SSTables are never re-compacted. The billion-row table serves p99 reads in <5ms.

examples.title: IoT Sensor Time Series
examples.description: An IoT platform stores sensor readings from 10 million devices, each reporting every second. Cassandra partitioned by (device_id, year_month) with clustering columns (timestamp DESC). The year_month bucket bounds partition size to ~2.6M rows/month per device maximum. TWCS compaction with a 1-day window groups same-day SSTables together; old windows are never recompacted. The write throughput of 10 million inserts/second is handled by the distributed ring—with 100 nodes at RF=3, each node handles 300K inserts/second, well within single-node capacity.

keyTakeaways: Cassandra's masterless ring provides linear horizontal scalability and no SPOF—adding nodes increases capacity proportionally
LSM-tree storage makes writes extremely fast; reads may require checking multiple SSTables—tune compaction for read/write balance
Data modeling is query-first and denormalized—design tables for specific query patterns, not normalized data relationships
Tunable consistency allows trading availability for consistency per-operation—CL.QUORUM for correctness, CL.ONE for maximum availability
Repair is the most critical operational responsibility—run it more frequently than gc_grace_seconds to prevent zombie data
TimeWindowCompaction is essential for time-series data—never mix TWCS with workloads that update old time windows
LWT provides linearizable transactions but costs 4 round-trips—use sparingly for correctness-critical operations
whyItMatters: Cassandra is the database of choice for high-availability, geographically distributed workloads where write throughput and linear scalability matter more than relational query flexibility. Netflix, Apple, Instagram, and Uber use Cassandra for their most demanding workloads. Understanding its trade-offs—eventual consistency, query-first modeling, repair requirements—is essential for evaluating when Cassandra is the right tool and designing schemas that perform well at scale.
reflectionQuestions: Design a Cassandra schema for a social media application where you need to: (a) get a user's posts in reverse chronological order, (b) find all posts tagged with a specific hashtag, and (c) get the top 10 trending posts. How many tables do you need?
A Cassandra cluster is experiencing high read latency that correlates with high compaction pending tasks. Walk through the diagnosis and remediation.
Explain the gc_grace_seconds setting. What happens if a replica is down for longer than gc_grace_seconds? How do you prevent this scenario?
Compare Cassandra and DynamoDB for a multi-region, high-write-throughput workload. What are the operational and architectural trade-offs?
numbersToKnow: Cassandra write latency: typically 0.5-2ms p99 at CL.LOCAL_QUORUM on well-tuned clusters
Max recommended partition size: 100MB; alert at 10MB, investigate at 50MB
gc_grace_seconds default: 864000 (10 days); run repair more frequently than this
LWT cost: 4 round-trips (Paxos prepare, promise, propose, commit); 10-20x regular write latency
Replication factor: 3 per datacenter is standard; 5 for highest availability requirements
Bloom filter false positive rate: 0.1% default; tune per table based on read-to-write ratio
